title: Answerability-Gain Rewards for Evidence-Label-Free GRU-Mem Gating: An Empirical Investigation

contributions.purpose: Replace expensive evidence-position labels for training GRU-Mem update/exit gates in recurrent memory agents.
contributions.mechanism: Answerability-gain rewards, a dense per-chunk signal measuring the change in answer confidence (teacher-forced log-likelihood of the correct answer) after each memory update, combined with per-step cost penalties for early exit.
contributions.evaluation: Evaluated on RULER-QA across context lengths from 28K to 224K tokens against outcome-only reward baselines.
contributions.source_quote: We propose answerability-gain rewards as a dense, evidence-label-free signal for training GRU-Mem gating mechanisms, measuring the change in answer confidence after each memory update.

contributions.purpose: Rigorously test whether dense answerability-gain rewards outperform simpler outcome-only rewards.
contributions.mechanism: Comprehensive experiments on RULER-QA (28K-224K tokens) comparing answerability-gain against outcome-only reward training across eight evaluation conditions.
contributions.evaluation: Negative result: 63.19% vs 63.48% average exact match with a 4-4 win/loss split, showing no consistent improvement over outcome-only rewards.
contributions.source_quote: We conduct comprehensive experiments showing that this approach does not consistently improve over outcome-only rewards, providing a rigorous negative result that informs future research directions.

contributions.purpose: Explain why the dense reward fails and point to remedies.
contributions.mechanism: Analysis identifying an early-exit bias: the answerability-gain signal biases the agent toward exiting after encountering the first piece of evidence, hurting multi-hop questions requiring integration of multiple evidence pieces.
contributions.evaluation: The identified limitation explains the negative result; the paper suggests multi-step lookahead rewards or evidence-diversity bonuses as alternatives.
contributions.source_quote: We identify an architectural limitation—early-exit bias after first evidence—that explains the negative result and suggests alternative approaches such as multi-step lookahead rewards or evidence-diversity bonuses.

self_declared_provenance.quote: Our work builds on the GRU-Mem architecture but investigates alternative reward signals for training the gating mechanisms without requiring evidence-position labels.

Our answerability-gain reward follows this line of research by providing per-chunk feedback based on answer confidence changes, though our results suggest this particular formulation does not consistently improve gate training.

Our exit gate mechanism shares conceptual similarities with these approaches but operates at the chunk level rather than the layer level, deciding when sufficient evidence has been gathered to answer a question.

notes: Explicit self-declared negative-result paper: the proposed dense reward does not consistently beat outcome-only rewards (63.19% vs 63.48%, 4-4 win/loss split). Builds directly on GRU-Mem (Sheng et al., 2026).
